analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to average 33 mpg by 2016, cutting U.S. oil use for driving by 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 109 House members from both parties, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to write fuel economy rules requiring cars made after model year 2015 to average at least 33 miles per gallon, which the bill's title says would cut the oil burned by American cars by 10 percent starting in 2016 [S2][S3]. It let regulators set separate standards for vehicles of different sizes so trucks and small cars could be treated differently, and required the rules to protect occupant safety and auto-manufacturing jobs [S3]. It also created a system letting one automaker sell fuel-economy credits to another [S2][S3]. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing and no vote until the two-year Congress expired [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers would spend less at the gas pump, and the country would use roughly 10 percent less oil for cars. The bill's text also tried to shield auto workers by requiring the new rules to maximize retention of U.S. auto manufacturing jobs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires automakers' fleets to average at least 33 miles per gallon for model years after 2015, which the bill's title says would cut U.S. automobile oil use by 10 percent beginning in 2016 [S2][S3].
Requires that fuel economy improvements not degrade vehicle safety and that the rules maximize retention of U.S. auto manufacturing jobs [S3].
Lets regulators set different standards for different vehicle size classes, so compliance could be tailored rather than one-size-fits-all [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, especially those selling less efficient fleets, would bear the cost of engineering and selling higher-mileage vehicles, and some of that cost would likely show up in new-vehicle prices. Oil companies would face reduced gasoline demand.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would likely raise new-car prices, and the bill does not provide direct consumer rebates or assistance to offset them [S3].

The credit-trading program could let manufacturers that sell mostly efficient cars profit while slower-moving competitors buy their way out of making their own fleets efficient, softening the oil savings [S2][S3].

Tighter fuel economy rules historically raised concerns that manufacturers would meet them by building smaller, lighter vehicles; the bill tries to answer this by requiring standards not to degrade safety, but the tension between mileage and vehicle weight is a real engineering constraint [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fuel savings to millions of drivers and the cut in oil dependence are broad and lasting, while the costs fall on automakers and partly on new-car buyers. The bill attempts to blunt the classic objections by building in safety and job protections, and its biggest design weakness is the credit-trading loophole, which could dilute the mandate. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs, but the oil-savings target depends on how strictly the Transportation Secretary writes the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Sherwood Boehlert introduced the bill on September 14, 2005, joined by 23 original cosponsors including Ed Markey, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that day [S3][S5].
Five days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and no further action of any kind was recorded for the rest of the 109th Congress [S5].

Despite 109 cosponsors, 80 Democrats, 28 Republicans, and 1 Independent, the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers were spared mandatory 33 mpg fleet standards, and oil producers kept demand roughly 10 percent higher than the bill would have allowed. Drivers, meanwhile, continued paying for the fuel the bill would have saved.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Joe Barton, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing or scheduled a vote on it; the same applied to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, where the bill was sent five days after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was bipartisan, with 80 Democrats and 28 Republicans among 109 total, but no votes were ever taken, so the record shows no party split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would force them to engineer and sell fleets averaging 33 mpg, a major cost for manufacturers of less efficient lineups. The bill tried to soften this with size-based standards, job-retention language, and tradeable credits [S2][S3].
A 10 percent cut in automobile fuel use means a lasting drop in gasoline demand, which is the bill's stated purpose [S1][S3].
Manufacturers already selling high-mileage fleets, and firms supplying efficiency technology, would gain market advantage and a new credit-trading revenue stream under the bill [S2][S3].
